chapters.name: Chapter 1: Using AI wisely in ministry

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Where AI helps a congregation, and where it does not
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Sort ministry tasks into "AI can draft this" and "people only".
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of ministry tasks, you will sort them into "AI can draft this" and "people only", keeping pastoral care, prayer requests and decisions about people with people.
An AI assistant, such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini, is a computer program you chat with in everyday words. It writes drafts, lists and plans in seconds.
In a congregation, it is useful for office work: weekly announcements, bulletin text, newsletters, event plans, volunteer sign-up messages, thank-you notes to donors and first drafts of grant applications.
It should not replace people in pastoral care, prayer requests, counseling, confession, conflict between members, or decisions about who serves or who receives help. Those need a trusted person, not a program.
Words to know:
- AI assistant: a computer program you chat with by typing or talking; it writes answers back.
- Pastoral care: the personal care a faith leader gives members: visits, counsel, comfort and prayer.
Try it now: List ten tasks your congregation's office does in a month. Mark each one "AI can draft" or "people only".
You can now name the ministry tasks where AI can help and the ones that must stay with people.

check.q: Which is a good office task for AI in a congregation?
check.why: AI helps with office writing; pastoral care and decisions need a trusted person.

check.q: A member asks if AI can counsel them about their grief. What do you say?
options: No; that needs a trusted person, not a program
check.why: Counseling and pastoral care need a trusted person.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Writing simple ground rules for AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a short "How we use AI" note your leaders can agree on.
This lesson builds toward: For your congregation's leaders, you will write a one-page "How we use AI" note that answers the four ground-rule questions, in plain words, ready for your board, elders or council to agree on.
Before staff and volunteers use AI, agree on a few simple rules. This keeps everyone safe and avoids surprises.
A good note answers four questions: What may we use AI for? What must never go into AI (names, prayer requests, giving records, health or family details)? Who reviews AI drafts before they are shared? Do we tell people when AI helped write something?
Keep it to one page and in plain words. Share it with your board, elders or ministry council and review it once a year.
Step by step:
- List the tasks AI may help with.
- List what must never be typed into AI.
- Name who reviews every AI draft before it is shared.
- Decide whether and how you say that AI helped.
- Get your leaders to agree and set a yearly review date.
Words to know:
- Ground rules: a short list of agreed rules everyone follows.
- Review: reading a draft carefully and fixing it before it is shared.
Try it now: Draft your congregation's one-page "How we use AI" note by answering the four questions. You may ask an AI assistant to make your draft clearer, but write the rules yourself.
You can now write a short set of AI ground rules for a congregation or faith-based program.

check.q: Which question does a "How we use AI" note answer?
options: Who reviews AI drafts before they are shared
check.why: The note answers what AI is for, what never goes in, who reviews and whether you tell people.

check.q: Your ministry team wrote AI ground rules. What do you do next?
options: Share them with your board, elders or council and review them each year
check.why: Leaders agree to the note, and it is reviewed once a year.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Keeping member information private
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn a request that has private details into a safe prompt with placeholders.
This lesson builds toward: Given a request that contains member information, you will rewrite it as a safe prompt with placeholders, with no names, prayer requests, giving records, health or contact details.
Members trust you with private things: prayer requests, illness, family troubles, giving amounts, addresses and phone numbers. Many AI tools may keep what you type, so treat a prompt like a postcard anyone could read.
Never type names, prayer requests, giving records, health details, children's information or contact details into an AI assistant. Use placeholders such as [member name] or [amount] and fill them in yourself afterward, in your own document.
If your organization pays for a business or education version of an AI tool, ask your administrator what its privacy settings are. Even then, keep confidential pastoral matters out.
Step by step:
- Write what you want the AI to help with.
- Read it for names, amounts, health, family and contact details.
- Replace each one with a placeholder like [member name].
- Send the prompt, then fill in the real details yourself outside the AI tool.
Words to know:
- Placeholder: a stand-in such as [member name] that you replace with the real detail later.
- Confidential: private information shared in trust that must not be passed on.
Try it now: Take this request: "Write a get-well card for Sister Mary Jones, who had heart surgery at County Hospital." Rewrite it with placeholders so no private detail goes into the AI, then send it.
You can now remove private member details from a prompt and use placeholders instead.

check.q: Why treat a prompt like a postcard?
options: Many AI tools may keep what you type
check.why: Many AI tools may keep what you type, so assume someone could read it.

check.q: You want AI to help write a get-well card for a member in the hospital. What do you type?
options: "Write a short get-well card for [member name] from our congregation."
check.why: Use placeholders and fill in the real details yourself afterward.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Putting AI to work for your congregation

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Drafting announcements and bulletins
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use a clear prompt to draft a weekly announcement in your congregation's voice.
This lesson builds toward: Given this week's events, you will write a clear prompt and draft a weekly announcement in your congregation's voice, with every date, time and place checked by you.
A clear prompt gets a better draft. Tell the AI what you need, a little about your congregation (no private details), and how you want it written.
For example: "Write a warm, short announcement for our Sunday bulletin. Events: food pantry Saturday 9 am to noon, youth group Wednesday 6 pm, choir needs two more voices. Friendly, welcoming tone, under 120 words."
Then ask for changes: "Make it shorter." "Add a line welcoming visitors." "Use simpler words." Check every date, time and place yourself before it goes out.
Step by step:
- List the events with dates, times and places.
- Say the tone you want and the length.
- Ask the AI for a draft.
- Ask for one or two changes.
- Check every date, time and place against your calendar.
Words to know:
- Prompt: what you type or say to an AI assistant to ask for something.
- Tone: how writing sounds: warm, formal, joyful, calm.
Try it now: Write a prompt for this week's real announcements at your congregation or program. Get a draft, ask for one change, then check every date and time against your calendar.
You can now draft a congregation announcement with AI and check it before it is shared.

check.q: What three things does a clear announcement prompt tell the AI?
options: What you need, a little about your congregation, and how you want it written
check.why: Tell the AI what you need, about your congregation (no private details) and how it should be written.

check.q: The draft is good but too long for the bulletin. What do you ask?
check.why: Ask for changes like "Make it shorter" until it fits.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Planning volunteer schedules and events
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to build a volunteer schedule with roles and placeholders, not names.
This lesson builds toward: Given roles, dates and how many people each needs, you will create a volunteer schedule with AI using placeholders instead of names, with real names added only in your own document.
Ushers, greeters, nursery helpers, food pantry teams and drivers all need schedules. AI can turn a list of roles and dates into a clear table in seconds.
Give it roles, dates and how many people each role needs, and use [Volunteer 1], [Volunteer 2] instead of real names. Then copy the table into your own document or spreadsheet and add names there.
AI can also make event checklists, for example for a revival, a fundraising dinner or a community health fair: what to do six weeks, two weeks and one day before.
Step by step:
- List the roles and how many people each needs.
- List the dates.
- Ask the AI for a table using [Volunteer 1], [Volunteer 2] placeholders.
- Copy it into your own document and add real names there.
- Ask for an event checklist if you are planning an event.
Words to know:
- Table: information set out in rows and columns.
- Checklist: a list of tasks you tick off as they are done.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant for a four-week schedule for three roles (for example greeter, usher, nursery) with two people each, using placeholders. Copy it into your own document.
You can now make a volunteer schedule and event checklist with AI while keeping names private.

check.q: What do you give AI to build a volunteer schedule?
options: Roles, dates and how many people each role needs
check.why: Give roles, dates and numbers needed, with placeholders instead of names.

check.q: You are planning a fundraising dinner. What can AI make for you?
options: The final guest list with names
A checklist of what to do six weeks, two weeks and one day before
check.why: AI can make event checklists by time before the event.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Checking drafts for faith, accuracy and tone
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Review an AI draft and fix anything that does not fit your tradition, facts or voice.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI draft, you will check it for faith, accuracy and tone and fix what does not fit, with scripture checked in your own sacred texts before a named reviewer approves it.
AI can make mistakes. It may quote a scripture wrongly, use words from a different tradition, get a holy day wrong, or sound stiff. It can also make up facts that sound true.
Read every draft for three things: faith (does it fit our beliefs and words?), accuracy (are quotes, dates and facts right?), and tone (does it sound like us and treat everyone with respect?). Check scripture and teachings in your own sacred texts, not in the AI.
If your organization is a tax-exempt charity, AI drafts should not endorse or oppose political candidates. The IRS explains the rules for churches and religious organizations in Publication 1828; ask your leaders or an advisor if you are unsure.
Step by step:
- Read for faith: does it match our beliefs and words?
- Check every quote, scripture and date in your own sources.
- Read it out loud for tone.
- Fix what is wrong, and note what you changed.
- Have the agreed reviewer approve it.
Words to know:
- Hallucination: when an AI writes something that sounds true but is made up.
- Tax-exempt: an organization the IRS recognizes as not paying federal income tax, with rules it must follow.
Official sources:
- IRS Publication 1828, Tax Guide for Churches and Religious Organizations
Try it now: Final task: draft your "How we use AI" note, then use AI to draft this week's announcement and a volunteer schedule with placeholders. Review both for faith, accuracy and tone, and mark what you changed.
You can now review AI drafts for faith, accuracy and tone before they reach your congregation.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds "How we use AI" note The note misses what must never go into AI, or who reviews. One page in plain words that answers all four questions. Lists the leaders who will agree to it and a yearly review date. Clear announcement A date, time or place is wrong or missing. This week's announcement drafted from a clear prompt, every detail checked. Warm and welcoming, and sounds like the congregation. Private volunteer schedule Real names or contact details went into the AI. Schedule with roles, dates and placeholders; names added in your own document. Also includes an event checklist by time before the event. Faith, accuracy and tone review A wrong quote, date or word from another tradition is left in. Both drafts checked for faith, accuracy and tone, and changes are marked. Scripture checked in your own sacred text, with the reference noted. Member privacy Any prayer request, giving record or member detail was typed into AI. Only placeholders were used in every prompt. Can show the safe prompt next to the original request. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What are the three review checks in this course?
check.why: Read every draft for faith, accuracy and tone.

check.q: The AI draft gets the date of a holy day wrong. What do you do?
options: Ask AI if it is sure
Remove the holy day from the calendar
Check it against your own tradition's calendar and fix it
check.why: AI may get a holy day wrong, so check and fix it yourself.
